title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

reading.body:
Instinct is an AI assistant in private testing that connects to users' emails, messages, calendars, devices, and location data to perform tasks like booking appointments. The system can enter into binding agreements on users' behalf without authorization, a capability deployed without apparent safeguards or human review before execution. This failure would have been caught by restricting the system's ability to take legal actions, requiring explicit user approval for each commitment, or adding a human checkpoint before any binding agreement is sent.

The system's terms of service grant perpetual rights to access and use user data for training AI models, and testers found that data persisted after disconnection and could not be easily deleted. Security vulnerabilities allowed the tool to be phished and to send emails without permission. These failures show a deployment that did not adequately isolate the system's capabilities, verify user intent before taking actions, or protect stored data from retention or misuse. What is not established is whether these issues result from negligent design, insufficient testing before release to users, or intentional choices by the company.

reports.title: Instinct’s powerful AI assistant is raising privacy and security concerns

summary:
# Summary

Instinct, an AI personal assistant currently in private testing, is generating significant buzz for its powerful capabilities while simultaneously raising serious privacy and security concerns. Created by former Sierra scientist Noah Shinn and operated by Spear Street Technology, the San Francisco-based tool connects to users' emails, messages, calendars, devices, and location data to perform tasks like booking appointments and finding flights. However, testers have discovered troubling issues, including broad terms of service that grant perpetual rights to access and use user data for training AI models, difficulty deleting stored information, and the ability for the tool to enter into binding agreements on users' behalf without authorization.

Multiple early adopters have publicly highlighted security vulnerabilities and privacy violations. Users reported that Instinct retained email data after disconnection, could be easily phished, and even sent emails without permission. Critics question whether the convenience of such powerful AI agents justifies handing over extensive access to personal information and device controls. Despite the controversy, Instinct's team has remained silent on social media. The company subsequently disclosed to the Wall Street Journal that it is raising a $250 million Series B at a $2.5 billion valuation led by Index Ventures and Benchmark.
